extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) who prosecute applications before the USPTO and handle petitions and PTAB appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and procedural standards for deciding when to file petitions versus appeals, preparing appeal briefs and replies, conducting hearings, and post-decision strategy before the PTAB. Focused on prosecution-stage decision making to obtain appropriate claim scope and maximize patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal vs. Petition — proper route
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of thumb is that a rejection of claims is to be appealed to the PTAB while objections and procedural requirements are subject to petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals are for adverse decisions on claims; many discretionary, procedural or non‑substantive examiner decisions traditionally are settled by petition. See 35 U.S.C. § 6(b) and MPEP Chapter 1000 for officials who decide which issues. Identify whether the examiner action is directly connected with merits of claim rejections or is procedural before choosing appeal or petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition generally has five points:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: • The petition must be in writing (37 CFR § 1.2). • The petition must contain a statement of facts involved, the point(s) to be reviewed and the action requested (37 CFR § 1.181(b)). • The petition must be accompanied by a fee, if required (37 CFR § 1.181(d)). • The petition must be timely filed (37 CFR § 1.181(f) or as required by specific statute/regulation). • The petition must comply with any specific statutory, regulatory or USPTO policy requirements. Failure to satisfy these can result in summary dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common petitionable situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of examiner actions that are subject to petition rather than appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common situations include final restriction requirements, refusal to enter an amendment or an affidavit after final rejection, premature final rejection, requirements to amend drawings, and petitions to revive applications/patents from abandonment or for non‑payment of maintenance fees. Consult the USPTO website summary of petition types and fees (the paper recommends the USPTO petition resource covering ~26 petition types) to determine the correct rule and fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-appeal readiness — focus on claims and finalized record
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals before the PTAB must focus on the claims, not the disclosed invention, and the record at the time the Appeal Brief is filed should be finalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoroughly review each claim (each independent claim) and the prosecution record to ensure the claims are of the correct scope and all evidence to be relied upon is properly entered and considered by the examiner. Opportunities to present additional evidence after filing a Notice of Appeal are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard — broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO applies the broadest reasonable meaning of claim words as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account guidance in the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examiners and PTAB panels may construe claims broadly, practitioners must step back to determine how broad claims will be read under the BRI/consistent-with-spec standard (In re Morris). This affects what to argue and whether amendments are needed prior to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure evidence is properly entered and addressed on the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence by an examiner does not mean evidence has been entered; the record must show evidence was entered and considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence is acknowledged but not meaningfully discussed by the examiner, insist (via response or supervisory review) that the examiner set forth on the record a reasoned explanation why the evidence is not persuasive. Cases sent to the PTAB where the examiner is silent about record evidence will often be remanded for consideration, delaying decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the Examiner and choose the right battle (use examiner statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the type of Examiner and whether negotiating via appeal/pre-appeal is helpful; use examiner-level data to pick when to appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal early and often can be effective, especially if examiner behavior indicates they prefer written advocacy or are unlikely to agree in interviews. The authors recommend using examiner interview/allowance statistics (e.g., <60% allowance after interviews may indicate written advocacy is preferable) and examiner/PTAB data to decide whether to pursue pre-appeal or appeal routes to 'change' the decision-makers and normalize idiosyncratic primary examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pre-Appeal Brief Conference — suitability, pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: A Pre-Appeal Brief Conference (pre-appeal review) is designed for cases where the examiner committed clear factual error; it has pros and cons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: two conferees review the case with the examiner. Cons: five-page limit may hamper arguing multiple rejections; Advisory Action may not provide specific feedback; if unsuccessful, a subsequent appeal conference may be pro forma. Consider potential briefing delays and impact on patent term adjustment (PTA) because Board clock starts when case is fully briefed and docketed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Brief — Summary of claimed subject matter (37 CFR § 41.37(c)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise summary for each independent claim involved in the appeal referring to the specification and drawings is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide claim chart tables tying claim elements to figures/paragraphs in the specification. For limitations that may be means/step-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), separately identify and analyze them — burden is on appellant to identify such limitations. Avoid 'mystery' words; be able to point to where claim language appears in the specification to avoid new matter or lack of written description problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure claim terms have antecedent/support in the specification; avoid new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms and phrases used in claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so meanings are ascertainable by reference to the description (37 CFR § 1.75(d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are amended to include language not explicitly in the original disclosure, make appropriate specification amendments concurrently (if needed) and explain how original disclosure provides written descriptive support. Adherence to this avoids new matter and written description rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Brief — Argument section: claim-by-claim and refined advocacy (37 CFR § 41.37(c)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments should be presented on a claim-by-claim basis, refined and expanded beyond prior prosecution responses; only arguments in the Appeal Brief will be considered by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not copy/paste the previous response. Use separate headings by ground of rejection and additional headings for different parts of your theory (e.g., failure to establish prima facie case, lack of suggestion/motivation, evidence of unexpected results). Avoid arguing by groups of claims — if claims are lumped, the panel will pick the most vulnerable claim as representative. Argue individual claims to maximize chances and patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame arguments as examiner 'error' and challenge examiner findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Couch arguments in terms of examiner error to address APJs' error‑focused review tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some APJs assume the examiner's rejection is correct and only review to the extent appellant urges error. Therefore identify and challenge examiner findings and conclusions explicitly. Also avoid chain citations of authority — a single on-point case is typically more persuasive. Rely on statute and case law rather than MPEP for merits issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's Answer — procedural and substantive review checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the Examiner's Answer for compliance with administrative guidance and on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to: whether the examiner accounted for all claims on appeal; whether a correct copy of the claims on appeal is present; whether the examiner repeated each rejection (if not repeated it may be treated as withdrawn); whether new evidence is relied upon in the Answer. If new evidence is present, consider objecting in the Reply Brief or petitioning to reopen prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to new evidence or novel legal positions in the Examiner's Answer
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner relies on additional evidence or asserts a new legal interpretation, take specific actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include objecting and responding substantively in a Reply Brief, petitioning (37 CFR § 1.181) for reopening if response requires amendments/evidence, or forwarding the matter to the TC Director and Deputy Commissioner for Patent Examination Policy if the Answer appears to forge new legal ground. Maintain one‑to‑one correspondence between your Appeal Brief arguments and the examiner's Response to Argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply Brief — focus on merits; use petition for procedural defects/new grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reply Brief should focus on merits issues; procedural anomalies (new grounds, admissibility, amendments) are generally resolved by petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner's Answer presents new arguments, you may respond in the Reply Brief (the Board must consider responsive arguments per In re Durance). But if full response requires amendments/evidence, file a petition that a new ground of rejection was improperly made. The time for filing a Reply Brief is tolled pending petition decision under the updated rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-decision procedure — monitoring docketing and forwarding
rubrics_metrics.description: Track the case on PAIR and ensure it has been forwarded/electronically transmitted to the PTAB for decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the IFW age, an electronic message notifies PTAB that the case is ready for decision. If you have not received a Docket Notice or notice of return to examiner shortly after briefing is completed, contact the examiner and request electronic forwarding to the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing — when to request and how to conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral argument can help but must be carefully prepared and is limited to the briefing content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request hearings when complex facts or cutting-edge legal issues are present; avoid hearings where only a §103 rejection exists without richer issues. Prepare a list of technical terms for the transcriptionist; note that you are typically limited to 20 minutes (panels may be lenient). Limit arguments to those in the briefs; avoid introducing new arguments. Avoid computer presentations — provide concise briefing packages and copies of key passages to panel members. Be ready to be interrupted with questions about claim scope and prior art and preface answers that raise issues not before the Board to avoid creating new grounds of rejection. Consider whether an applicant/assignee representative should attend (weigh ability to explain tech vs. risk of admissions). Be mindful of remote panelists and accessibility (e.g., color blindness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decision practice — rehearing, RCE, PTA and new grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: After the PTAB decision, examine what was affirmed/reversed, preserve PTA where possible, and pursue rehearing or reopening appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If decision reverses all rejections, proceed to allowance. If affirmed-in-part with at least one independent claim patentable, avoid filing an RCE (it may forfeit patent term adjustment); instead examiner should cancel affirmed claims and allow remaining claims. Compare panel reasoning to examiner's Answer to detect designated or undesignated new grounds of rejection. If you believe a new ground was made, raise it explicitly in a single request for rehearing (37 CFR § 41.52) and state arguments with particularity. If a new ground under 37 CFR § 41.50(b) is made, elect either to reopen prosecution or to request rehearing before the PTAB; you cannot pursue both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximizing patent term — claim strategy in briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful claim-by-claim argumentation can maximize patent term adjustment (PTA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separately argue dependent claims that seem likely to win so an appellate reversal on at least one claim may lead to PTA. Know the statutory and regulatory provisions tying appellate reversals to PTA (35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(C)(iii); 37 CFR § 1.702(e)). Consider that certain remands may also result in PTA.
